stem: An architecture review flags that a compromised application server in a shared subnet could currently reach every other resource in the VPC, with no restriction beyond the default security group. Which TWO changes add defense in depth without redesigning the VPC's subnets? (Select TWO.)

choices.text: Replace the default security group with one that allows only the specific ports the application needs
Remove the subnet's route table entirely so no traffic can be evaluated
Move the NAT gateway into the same subnet as the application server
Add a custom network ACL to the subnet with numbered rules that deny unexpected traffic
Disable the VPC's default network ACL so no rules apply

rationale: Replacing the default security group with one scoped to only the ports the application needs shrinks what the compromised server's resource-level allow list permits, limiting lateral movement to other resources. Adding a custom network ACL to the subnet layers a stateless, numbered-rule control above the security group, which is the subnet-level defense-in-depth layer the review is asking for. Removing the subnet's route table would break all connectivity, including legitimate traffic, rather than adding a security control, so it does not achieve defense in depth. Moving the NAT gateway into the same subnet changes where outbound internet traffic exits, but it does nothing to restrict east-west traffic between resources already inside the subnet. Disabling the default network ACL removes a filtering layer rather than adding one, which is the opposite of the goal, and a subnet's NACL association cannot simply be turned off without another NACL taking its place.
